item.title: Pack the repo, not the prompt
item.description:
Real repositories do not fit in a context window. Everyone who has pasted half a monorepo into a chat already knows this. The usual responses are worse than the problem: dump more files, raise the window, or hope the model guesses the right path. I got tired of that, so I wrote a local indexer that walks the tree once and only packs what the task needs.

The window is not the repo

A 128k window is a billing feature. It is not a map of the code. Even when the window is huge, stuffing it full of tests, snapshots, generated fixtures, and three copies of the same helper does not make the model more oriented. It makes the relevant function sit in the middle of noise. Agents fail in boring ways here. They edit the test that mentioned the symbol instead of the implementation. They miss the import graph. They hallucinate a file that would have been obvious if the outline had been in the prompt instead of a random grep.

Hand-picking files does not scale past a few thousand lines. You do it for an afternoon and then you start skipping the boring packages, which is exactly where the bug is. I wanted something I could point at a tree I do not already hold in my head.

Index once

grasp walks the repo, honors `.gitignore`, skips binaries, and builds an index: symbols, imports, an import graph, chunked source, a BM25 text index. It writes `.grasp/index.json`. That is the whole trick. Run `grasp index` after significant changes. Nothing watches the tree live, on purpose. A silent reindex in the middle of a refactor is a good way to search yesterday's names.

I pointed it at `facebook/react` while building it: 7,226 files, 88,854 chunks, indexed in about fifteen seconds on a laptop. That number is a calibration, not a benchmark claim for your machine. It is enough to know this is not a toy that only works on the blog's own repo.

Zero runtime dependencies. Node's own `fs`, `path`, and `crypto`. You can `npm i -g @zent7x/grasp` or `npx @zent7x/grasp index` from inside the repository you want it to understand. CLI for your shell, or an MCP server over stdio when an editor or an agent needs the same context on demand.

Ask, then pack

`grasp ask` ranks chunks against a task and prints `path:Lstart-Lend [symbol] score`. The score is BM25, boosted when a query term matches a symbol name, boosted again when a top hit is graph-adjacent to another top hit. That last part matters. A function is rarely the whole story. The caller two files over is usually the reason you asked.

`grasp pack` is the thing I actually paste. Same ranking, but the output is a Markdown bundle of real source, packed greedily up to a token budget. `--budget 8000 --out context.md` is a typical invocation. Drop `--out` and it prints. This is what `grasp_pack` returns over MCP. It is not a summary. Summaries are how you lose the line that had the bug. It is the source, truncated by relevance instead of by hope.

`grasp outline` is the other door. A compact, directory-grouped symbol tree. Every function, class, and const it found, with line ranges, no bodies. When I do not know what to ask yet, I read the outline first. Asking a vague question of a 7,000-file tree is how you get a vague pack.

Noise is the default

Test, fixture, snapshot, and example files are demoted unless you pass `--tests`. Otherwise the pack fills with the files that mention the words most often, which in a healthy repo is the test suite. The implementation then ranks under the noise, and the agent 'helps' by rewriting an assertion. I would rather miss a test name than miss `src/`. You can turn the demotion off when the task is the tests. The default is the opposite of dump-everything, because dump-everything is how we got here.

There is a TUI if you want to poke the index with your hands: `grasp tui`. Type a query, open a chunk, pack the top results, quit. Color on a TTY, `NO_COLOR=1` when you do not want it. I use the CLI more than the TUI. The TUI is for the days when I do not yet know the name of the thing I am hunting.

Local, on purpose

grasp runs on your machine. The index is a file in the repo's working tree, not a cloud. That is the same reason tally is one HTML file and cogrep does not phone home. I do not want a third party holding a map of a private codebase so an agent can be slightly more helpful. If the job is 'give the model the right source', the right source can be selected offline.

This pairs with routing.run more than it looks. One tool decides what text leaves your disk. The other refuses to keep that text once it is in flight. I do not want a world where we carefully pack a prompt and then a router writes it down. Pack the repo. Forget the prompt. The rest is models, and models are a commodity.

If you want the commands, they are in the README. If you want the position, it is this. Do not throw the tree at the window. Build a map, ask a question, pack only what the question needs. Then go write the patch. The agent can come along. It does not get to eat the whole company to do it.

item.title: Real Chromium pixels in your terminal
item.description:
Terminal browsers usually cheat. They parse HTML, throw away the layout, and print what survives. That works for reading a man page online and falls apart the moment a page depends on its real rendering, which in 2026 is nearly every page.

The cheat

Lynx, w3m, and the modern copies of that idea are text-mode browsers. They download the document, keep the strings, and invent a layout that fits a grid of cells. Images become `[IMG]`. CSS becomes a suggestion. JavaScript becomes a problem you ignore. For a page that is a document, this is fine. For a page that is an application, it is a different product pretending to be a browser.

I kept reaching for those tools anyway. My work lives in a terminal. The editor is there, the git graph is there, the agent loop is there. Opening Chrome to check a preview, a dashboard, or a docs page meant leaving the place I was already thinking. A hundred times a day is not a workflow. It is a tax.

So I looked at what a terminal can actually display now. Ghostty speaks the Kitty graphics protocol. That protocol is not a screenshot pasted into the scrollback. It is a way to put pixels in the same grid as your text, then keep using the terminal as a terminal. Splits, keybindings, and scrollback still belong to Ghostty. The page is just another kind of cell content.

Real pixels

terminal-fenster takes the other road. Chromium renders the page offscreen, for real. A Rust core converts each frame into terminal graphics and writes it through Kitty. The engine is Electron with the sandbox on. There is no Node in the page, no context leak, no DevTools port hanging off localhost. The control socket is mode 0600 inside a directory that is 0700. Nothing in this stack is a toy HTML parser with extra steps.

That screenshot is a Ghostty capture on macOS. The page is the page. Flexbox, webfonts, canvas, and the rest of the 2026 web survive because Chromium is drawing them. If a site needs a real engine, it gets a real engine. The terminal is the window, not the renderer.

I wrote this down in public because the other demos in this category usually hide the cost. A full-viewport repaint at 2108×1406 on the old direct path was about 7 frames a second. Encoding was not the bottleneck. Getting a huge bitmap through a PTY was. The current compositor keeps a retained RGB canvas, tiles the damage, and uses shared memory for dense local repaints when the terminal will take it. Sparse updates are small. The honest number for displayed frames per second on a busy full-viewport animation is still a release gate, not a marketing line. The status page says what is verified and what is not.

Input the other way

Pixels without input is a slideshow. Keys and clicks in the terminal are mapped back into Chromium events. You can scroll, click, type, fill a form, and log in without leaving the shell. Mouse coordinates come in as pixels when the terminal speaks SGR-Pixels, and as cells when it does not. iTerm2 reports SGR-Pixels as permanently reset, so treating those as pixels would collapse the whole page into the top-left corner. The pointer mapping has to know the difference. The e2e suite clicks a target and asserts the pixels under the cursor actually changed. A click that does not move paint is a lie.

Ctrl+q quits. Ctrl+l opens a URL. Ctrl+f finds in the page. Tabs exist, up to sixteen, with a strip that belongs to the terminal rather than to a fake browser chrome floating on top of it. MCP sessions stay single-tab and isolated from the interactive session on purpose. An agent driving a browser should not share cookies with the one I am looking at.

Why Ghostty, and what that does not mean

Ghostty on macOS is the configuration I have actually driven end to end. Kitty and WezTerm speak the same graphics protocol and should work. I have not sat in those terminals and signed that off. Apple Terminal has no graphics protocol, so interactive `open` refuses it and points you at `--headless`. Headless is the right mode for scripts, CI, and agents. It is not a secret second product. It is the same engine without a PTY to paint into.

The name is German for terminal window. I meant it literally. A terminal window that is also a browser window, not a text approximation of one. If you want the source, it is on GitHub. MIT. No signed binaries yet, no `curl | bash` release, no claim that Linux interactive rendering is as proven as the macOS Ghostty path. Experimental source alpha is the true status. I would rather write that twice than ship a download that pretends otherwise.

What this is for

I built it because switching to a browser window was the most annoying part of a day spent in a terminal. Docs, previews, a sticky admin page, a local dashboard that only exists on localhost. Those are the jobs. It is not a daily-driver replacement for a full browser until signing, memory, and terminal coverage say so. Chromium still has a memory floor. A short about:blank probe on the engine was in the hundreds of megabytes of summed RSS. That is the cost of a real engine, and I am not going to hide it behind a GIF.

If you work the way I do, the useful test is simple. Open the page you keep alt-tabbing to. If it looks like the page, and you can click it, the experiment worked. If it does not, file it against the source, not against a landing page. The landing page is here. The writing is this post. The code is the thing that has to be true.

item.title: Zero prompt logging is the product
item.description:
An LLM router sits in the most sensitive spot of the whole stack. Every prompt, every system message, and every tool result passes through it. Most providers treat that stream as an asset to mine. I think the mining is the bug.

The most sensitive hop

Once you put a router in front of more than one model, you have built a place that sees everything. The user prompt. The system prompt you did not want a vendor to keep. The tool result that contains a customer record. The stack trace from an internal admin. There is no version of this job that sees less. The only decision is whether that stream becomes a dataset.

Vendors have a story for why it should. They will improve the model. They will debug your latency. They will train a classifier that catches abuse. Some of that is real operations. Most of it is a business model that needs your context more than you need their model. The model is replaceable. The context is not.

What routing.run actually does

routing.run is OpenAI compatible on the outside. You change a base URL and an API key. The tools you already have keep talking the same protocol. Inside, the request is routed to a healthy upstream, usage is recorded without the body, and the prompt is dropped. There is no prompt store to breach, subpoena, or train on, because the store does not exist.

That sentence is doing a lot of work, so I will be exact. Request content is processed so it can reach the selected provider. The provider still sees the prompt. I cannot unsee a model API. What I will not do is keep a second copy in my own logs, my own analytics warehouse, or a 'help us improve' bucket that is really a corpus. Usage logs hold the operational minimum: model, provider, tokens, latency, billing, and the security signals you need to keep the service up. Not the text.

The core is published under AGPL-3.0 for the same reason. A privacy claim you cannot inspect is just marketing. If you want to know how routing, usage, and provider selection actually work, read the code. I would rather be argued with about an implementation than believed about a landing page.

Commodity models, scarce context

The models themselves are a commodity now. They get cheaper and better every quarter no matter what I do. A new name lands, a new context window lands, a new price lands. If your product is 'we picked the right model', you are in a race you will lose on a press cycle. If your product is 'we will not keep your prompts', the race is different. You can change the upstream without changing the contract.

Failover is part of that contract. Providers go unhealthy. Streaming requests can only fail over before any response content has been shown to the client, otherwise you have forked a completion in front of the user. Ordered provider chains and circuit breakers exist so the router can move eligible work. They do not exist so I can justify keeping bodies around 'in case we need to replay'. Replay of a prompt is a storage decision. I declined it.

How to tell if a router is lying

Ask where the bodies go. If the answer is a dashboard with a search box, they are logging prompts. If the answer is 'we anonymize', ask what is left after anonymization, who can reverse it, and how long it lives. If the answer is 'we need it to improve quality', that is their business, not yours. If the answer is a privacy policy that takes four screens to say maybe, it is a maybe.

I built routing.run because I was tired of that conversation. Zero prompt logging is not a setting buried next to a cookie banner. It is the product. If a vendor needs your prompts to improve the model, that is their business, not yours. The FAQ on this site says the same thing in one line, and I will keep saying it until the default in this industry is forgetfulness rather than retention.

Billing is the other place bodies sneak back in. A usage line needs tokens, a model id, and a timestamp. It does not need the prompt. If a billing export contains customer text, the router is logging, whatever the privacy page says. I would rather explain a sparse invoice than explain a corpus.

If you want the operational details, they live on the product site, not here. This page is the position. The position is simple. The router in the middle sees everything. It should remember nothing. I ship from Kashmir, I quote in writing, and I will not take a job that needs me to hold your prompts in a database so a model vendor can get smarter on your customers. There are plenty of people who will. I am not one of them.

item.title: Authorized means written down
item.description:
Every security engagement I take starts the same way. A written scope that names the systems, the techniques, and the window. Not a verbal ok on a call. A document both sides can point at later.

Nothing starts on a call

A call is useful for tone. It is useless as authorization. People remember different sentences. Legal remembers none of them. If the work later has to be explained to a founder, a counsel, or a bug bounty platform, 'we talked about it' is not a record. The record is a document with names, URLs, IP ranges if they matter, excluded systems, allowed techniques, and a start and end. Both sides keep a copy. Then the work can start.

I will not begin recon before that document exists. Curiosity is not authorization. A public signup form is not authorization. A friend forwarding a URL in chat is not authorization. If you need that energy, look elsewhere. The FAQ on this site is blunt about it because I am tired of being asked to 'just have a look' at a production box that belongs to someone who did not write me an invitation.

What the document has to name

The systems. The techniques I may use. The techniques I may not. The window. The severity scale we will use when a finding lands. The channel for critical reports, which is never 'wait for the final PDF'. The rule for out-of-scope discoveries: stop, write it down, do not keep pulling that thread until someone expands the scope in writing. If a credential appears in a screenshot, it gets rotated, it does not get reused as a party trick.

I quote in writing after I understand the blast radius. If the quote is wrong for you, we stop there. No retainer hiding in the weeds, no 'discovery phase' that is actually the engagement without a scope. I work inside existing repos more often than I rewrite them. The rewrite is the job only when the rewrite is the job.

How the Publive work ran

The Publive engagement is the one I will name, because it was authorized, scoped, and reported in the open enough to be useful as an example. Scope first. Then recon against what the document allowed. Findings written up as they landed, each with reproduction steps and impact stated plainly, in language a product person could read without a decoder ring. Critical bugs were reported the day they were confirmed. They were not saved for a dramatic final report. A final report that sits on a finding for two weeks so the narrative lands better is a vanity document. I will not write one.

I am not going to publish those bugs here. This is not a writeup of someone else's production. It is a writeup of the method. The method is the thing you can reuse. The bugs belonged to Publive the moment they were confirmed, and they were told the same day.

A bug outside scope is a liability

People treat extra bugs as generosity. They are not. A finding on a system you were not asked to touch is an uninsured action. It can become a disclosure problem, a relationship problem, and in the worst case a legal problem, even if your intent was clean. I do not hunt friends, family, or random production boxes. I do not 'help' by continuing past the edge of the page. If I trip over something adjacent, I stop, I describe it without proof-of-concept theater, and I wait for a written expansion. If the expansion never comes, the note stays in the report as out of scope and I leave it alone.

That rule is how I sleep. It is also how I keep being allowed to do this work. Authorized security research is a small door. Walking through it without the paper is how people get the door closed on them, and on everyone else who does this carefully. I would rather leave a finding on the table than create a liability that the scope never covered.

If you want the work

Email zentex@warm.run. Put the problem in the first paragraph. Links beat PDFs. I will answer in writing: a scope, a no, or a few sharp questions. No intro call required. If I cannot help, I say so. If I can, nothing happens until the invitation exists on paper. Then I am happy to break things carefully.

Kashmir, IST, async by default. I build warm.run and routing.run in the same weeks I take this work, so I am selective. Selectivity is not a brand. It is how the scope stays honest. If that is too slow for you, there are firms with twenty people and a slide deck. I am one person with a terminal, and the paper comes first.
